Terroir · 4-minute read

Why Rioja tastes the way it does

Two climates that rarely meet share one sheltered valley. That is where Rioja's wines get their body, their colour and their acidity.

Source: Pliego de condiciones DOCa Rioja (Consejo Regulador copy, amendments to AM10), p. 15, 19

A valley with walls

The vineyards follow the Ebro for 100 km, from Haro in the west to Alfaro in the east, in a valley never more than about 40 km wide. They climb in terraces to about 700 m. The mountains around it make Rioja a natural region of its own, and the Sierra de Cantabria to the north protects the vines.

Three provinces share the vineyard: La Rioja, Álava and Navarra, 63,593 hectares across 144 municipalities.

On the mapHaro to Alfaro, the whole valleyOn the mapSierra de Cantabria
Source: Pliego de condiciones DOCa Rioja (Consejo Regulador copy, amendments to AM10), p. 15, 20

Cool in the west, warm in the east

The whole valley sits where the Atlantic and the Mediterranean meet, so temperatures stay mild and about 400 mm of rain falls in a year. Moving east, the climate turns Mediterranean and the wine changes with it.

Rioja Alta

Atlantic. More rain and fewer hours of sun than the south.

Wines of medium strength with body and high acidity, made for the barrel.

On the mapRioja Alta
Rioja Alavesa

Both climates meet. As sunny as Rioja Alta, a little drier, and the most sheltered by the Sierra de Cantabria.

A touch more alcohol and less acidity. Good young or aged.

On the mapRioja Alavesa
Rioja Oriental

Mediterranean. The least rain and the most sun. Older documents call it Rioja Baja.

More alcohol and extract. Used in blends for barrel ageing, and also drunk young.

On the mapRioja Oriental
Source: Pliego de condiciones DOCa Rioja (Consejo Regulador copy, amendments to AM10), p. 15, 20; Documento único PDO-ES-A0117, p. 5

Three soils, three weights

Clay-limestone covers a quarter of the vineyard, on terraces and small plots in Rioja Alavesa, the Sonsierra and parts of Rioja Alta. It is the main source of wines for ageing. Ferrous clay, red and rolling, covers another quarter. Alluvial soil near the rivers, flat, deep and full of stones, covers half. Both of these give wines with less body than the clay-limestone.

Most of Rioja's soil is balanced between sand, silt and clay, slightly alkaline, poor in organic matter, and holds a moderate amount of water through the summer.

On the mapClay-limestone terraces, Rioja Alavesa
Source: Pliego de condiciones DOCa Rioja (Consejo Regulador copy, amendments to AM10), p. 15, 16, 20

Made for the barrel

Wine is about a fifth of the region's economy, and Rioja's long focus on ageing has built one of the largest concentrations of oak barrels in the world. Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are the result: see Famous styles.

Rioja makes sparkling wine too. Wines "made by the Champagne method" from Rioja Alta and Alavesa were shown in Madrid in 1857, and in 1890 a French firm in Haro's station quarter hired a champagne maker from Reims. The cool end of the Winkler heat scale keeps the base wines fresh and acidic. Since 2017 the rules cover traditional-method sparkling whites and rosés.

On the mapHaro's station quarter
Source: Pliego de condiciones DOCa Rioja (Consejo Regulador copy, amendments to AM10), p. 19, 20

How it tastes

Reds

Purple when young, cherry-garnet as crianza, ruby-brick as gran reserva; intense fruit, toasted oak, then spice with age.

Whites

Pale straw with lemon-green rims; green fruit, flowers.

Rosés

Strawberry; red fruit, floral notes.

Source: Documento único PDO-ES-A0117 (EU single document, Rioja), p. 1

Zones

Rioja AltaAtlantic influence and more rain give reds of medium strength with body and high acidity, suited to barrel ageing.Rioja AlavesaAtlantic and Mediterranean climates meet behind the Sierra de Cantabria, giving slightly riper wines with a little less acidity, to drink young or age.Rioja OrientalA drier, warmer Mediterranean climate with more sun gives riper, fuller reds that suit blending and barrel ageing.
